Apple___Apple_scab.description: A common fungal disease of apple trees that causes dark, scabby spots on leaves and fruit.
steps: Prune trees to improve air circulation and sunlight penetration.
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to reduce spore survival.
Apply urea to fallen leaves to accelerate decomposition of infected tissue.
Use resistant varieties like Liberty, Enterprise, or Pristine.
Follow a preventative fungicide spray schedule, especially during wet spring weather.

fertilizer.recommendation: Apply a balanced fertilizer in early spring to support tree vigor. Avoid excessive nitrogen, which promotes lush growth susceptible to infection.

Apple___Apple_scab.irrigation: Water at the base of the tree using drip irrigation to keep foliage dry. Ensure deep watering during dry spells, especially from bloom to harvest.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Apple___Black_rot.description: A fungal disease that can cause leaf spots, fruit rot, and cankers on apple trees.
steps: Prune out and destroy all cankered and dead branches during dormancy.
Remove mummified (dried, shriveled) fruits from trees and the ground.
Practice proper sanitation by removing all plant debris.
Maintain tree health with proper watering and feeding to reduce stress.

fertilizer.recommendation: Maintain balanced nutrition with a soil test. High potassium levels can help with disease resistance.

Apple___Black_rot.irrigation: Avoid overhead watering. Use drip irrigation to keep the trunk and leaves dry. Water deeply and infrequently.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A fungal disease that requires both an apple and a juniper (cedar) to complete its life cycle, causing bright orange spots.
steps: Remove nearby eastern red cedar trees if possible (alternate host).
Plant resistant apple varieties like Liberty, William's Pride, or Freedom.
Apply protective fungicide sprays starting at the pink bud stage.
Monitor nearby cedar trees for orange, gelatinous galls in the spring.

fertilizer.recommendation: A healthy, well-fed tree is less susceptible. Apply a balanced fertilizer in the spring.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.irrigation: Water at the base of the tree. Keeping leaves dry is critical to prevent fungal spore germination.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Apple___healthy.description: The apple plant appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Prune annually during dormancy to maintain good air circulation and an open structure.
Monitor regularly for early signs of pests or diseases.
Use organic mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.
Thin fruit to one apple per cluster to promote larger, healthier fruit.

fertilizer.recommendation: Apply a balanced fertilizer in early spring before new growth begins. Base application rates on tree age and size.

Apple___healthy.irrigation: Water deeply once a week during the growing season, providing 1-2 inches of water. Use a soaker hose or drip irrigation.

pesticides: Dormant oil spray (late winter) to control overwintering pests.
insecticides: Insecticidal soap for aphids
Spinosad for codling moth

Blueberry___healthy.description: The blueberry plant appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Test soil and maintain an acidic pH (4.5-5.5) using soil acidifiers if necessary.
Use pine needle or oak leaf mulch to help maintain acidity and conserve moisture.
Prune older canes during dormancy to encourage vigorous new growth.
Protect bushes from birds with netting as fruit ripens.

fertilizer.recommendation: Use fertilizers formulated for acid-loving plants. Apply once in early spring and again after fruit has set.

Blueberry___healthy.irrigation: Blueberries have shallow roots and require consistent moisture. Provide 1-2 inches of water per week using drip irrigation.

pesticides: Sulfur sprays can help prevent fungal issues.
insecticides: Spinosad for fruit worms
Neem oil for aphids and other soft-bodied insects.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: A fungal disease that appears as white powdery spots on leaves and shoots of cherry trees.
steps: Prune to improve air circulation through the canopy, allowing leaves to dry faster.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which promotes susceptible new growth.
Remove and destroy infected shoots and leaves.
Choose planting sites with good sun exposure and air movement.

fertilizer.recommendation: Use a low-nitrogen, high-potassium fertilizer to support fruit development without encouraging excessive leafy growth.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.irrigation: Water at the base of the tree using a soaker hose or drip system. Avoid wetting the foliage.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: The cherry plant appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Prune annually during dormancy to maintain an open, productive structure.
Use mulch to conserve moisture and regulate soil temperature.
Monitor for pests like cherry fruit fly and aphids.
Protect the trunk from sunscald in winter with tree wrap.

fertilizer.recommendation: Apply a balanced, low-nitrogen fertilizer in early spring.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.irrigation: Water deeply during dry periods, especially during fruit development to prevent fruit drop and cracking.

pesticides: Fixed copper spray during dormancy to prevent canker.
insecticides: Spinosad for cherry fruit fly
Insecticidal soap for aphids.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: A fungal disease of corn characterized by long, narrow, rectangular lesions on the leaves.
steps: Use resistant corn hybrids when available.
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops like soybeans or wheat.
Plow under crop debris after harvest to reduce fungal inoculum.
Ensure proper plant spacing to improve air circulation and reduce humidity.
Scout fields regularly to monitor disease progression.

fertilizer.recommendation: Maintain balanced soil fertility, especially potassium levels, to enhance disease tolerance.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.irrigation: Avoid overhead irrigation, which wets leaves and promotes disease. If using sprinklers, water in the morning so leaves dry quickly.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust.description: A fungal disease causing small, cinnamon-brown pustules on corn leaves.
steps: Plant resistant hybrids adapted to your region; this is the primary management tool.
Time planting to avoid periods when peak spore production is likely.
Practice crop rotation to reduce disease carryover.
Maintain good air circulation through appropriate plant density.

fertilizer.recommendation: Adequate nutrition helps the plant tolerate infection. Follow recommendations from a soil test.
products: Nitrogen sidedressing before the V8 stage.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust.irrigation: Reduce leaf wetness duration by watering early in the day. Avoid overhead irrigation during cool, humid evenings.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: A fungal disease of corn that produces long, elliptical, grayish-green or tan lesions on the leaves.
steps: Use resistant corn hybrids with good tolerance ratings.
Plow under crop debris after harvest to reduce overwintering inoculum.
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops like soybeans or alfalfa.
Ensure proper plant spacing for good air circulation.
Scout fields regularly, especially during periods of high humidity and moderate temperatures.

fertilizer.recommendation: Ensure balanced nutrition, particularly adequate potassium, as it plays a role in disease resistance.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.irrigation: If irrigating, do so early in the day to allow leaves to dry quickly. Avoid late evening watering. Drip irrigation is preferable to overhead sprinklers.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: The corn plant appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Test soil and maintain pH between 6.0-6.8.
Use proper plant spacing (8-12 inches between plants) for optimal growth.
Control weeds, especially in the first 4-6 weeks, as they compete for nutrients and water.
Monitor for common pests like corn earworm and aphids.
Harvest when kernels are 'milky' for sweet corn.

fertilizer.recommendation: Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder. Apply a starter fertilizer at planting, then sidedress with nitrogen when plants are 12-18 inches tall.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.irrigation: Provide at least 1 inch of water per week, especially during the critical tasseling and silking stages.

pesticides: Preventative fungicides are typically not needed for healthy corn unless disease pressure is high.
insecticides: Spinosad for corn earworm (apply to silks)
Neem oil for aphids.

Grape___Black_rot.description: A serious fungal disease of grapes that can rot the fruit and cause leaf spots.
steps: Prune vines during dormancy to improve air circulation and sunlight penetration.
Remove and destroy mummified berries and infected canes.
Practice good sanitation throughout the season.
Use resistant grape varieties when available.
Follow a strict fungicide spray schedule from pre-bloom through berry development.

fertilizer.recommendation: Avoid excessive nitrogen, which creates a dense canopy. Ensure good potassium and magnesium levels.

Grape___Black_rot.irrigation: Use drip irrigation to deliver water directly to the soil. Keeping leaves, flowers, and fruit dry is essential.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: A complex fungal disease of grapevines that causes a variety of symptoms, including leaf spots and wood decay.
steps: Prune out and destroy infected wood showing 'tiger-stripe' patterns.
Protect large pruning wounds with a sealant or fungicidal paint.
Avoid severe pruning that creates large wounds, which are entry points for the fungus.
Remove and destroy severely infected vines to prevent spread.
Maintain balanced fertilization to promote overall vine health.

fertilizer.recommendation: Focus on balanced nutrition to reduce plant stress, which can trigger symptoms.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).irrigation: Provide consistent and deep watering to avoid drought stress, which can exacerbate the disease.

pesticides: No highly effective fungicides are available. Management relies on cultural practices. Some growers use lime sulfur or Trichoderma-based products on pruning wounds.
insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: A fungal disease causing angular, dark brown lesions on grape leaves, which can lead to defoliation.
steps: Prune to improve air circulation through the canopy.
Remove and destroy infected leaves and canes at the end of the season.
Ensure good weed control around the base of vines.
Start a protective fungicide program early in the season.

fertilizer.recommendation: A balanced nutrient supply helps vines tolerate minor infections.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.irrigation: Avoid overhead irrigation to reduce leaf wetness. Water at the soil level.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Grape___healthy.description: The grape vine appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Prune annually during dormancy to maintain proper vine structure and balance fruit production.
Train vines on a trellis for good air circulation and sun exposure.
Use cover crops between rows to improve soil health and prevent erosion.
Monitor for common pests like Japanese beetles and grape berry moth.

fertilizer.recommendation: Apply a balanced fertilizer in the spring based on a soil test. Grapes do not require heavy feeding.

Grape___healthy.irrigation: Water deeply during drought, especially from bloom until the berries begin to change color (veraison). Reduce water as harvest approaches to concentrate sugars.

insecticides: Kaolin clay for Japanese beetles
Spinosad for grape berry moth.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: A devastating bacterial disease of citrus trees, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, leading to yellow shoots and bitter fruit.
steps: Remove and destroy infected trees immediately to prevent spread to healthy trees.
Plant new trees only from certified disease-free nursery sources.
Implement area-wide management programs for the psyllid vector.
Use reflective mulches to deter the psyllid.
Support tree health with enhanced nutritional programs.

fertilizer.recommendation: Infected trees benefit from enhanced nutritional foliar sprays containing micronutrients like zinc, manganese, and iron to manage symptoms.
products: Foliar sprays of zinc sulfate and manganese sulfate

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).irrigation: Provide consistent water to avoid drought stress, which can worsen symptoms.

pesticides: No direct bactericide is effective. Control relies on managing the insect vector.
insecticides: Systemic insecticides like Imidacloprid
Horticultural oil sprays
Spinosad
Biological controls like the Tamarixia radiata wasp.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease causing dark, angular spots on peach leaves and fruit.
steps: Use resistant varieties like Clayton, Scarlet Pearl, or Summer Pearl.
Practice good sanitation by removing and destroying fallen leaves and fruit.
Prune to improve air circulation and allow for faster drying of foliage.
Avoid working with trees when they are wet.
Maintain tree vigor with proper fertilization and watering.

fertilizer.recommendation: Avoid excessive nitrogen. Ensure adequate levels of calcium and potassium.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.irrigation: Use drip irrigation to keep foliage dry. Water deeply during dry periods.

pesticides: Copper bactericides (applied during dormancy and before rain events)
insecticides: Not applicable for this bacterial disease.

Peach___healthy.description: The peach tree appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Prune annually during dormancy to maintain an open center (vase) shape for sunlight penetration.
Thin fruits to 6-8 inches apart when they are thumbnail-sized for proper size development.
Monitor for common pests like peach tree borers and oriental fruit moths.
Apply a dormant oil spray in late winter to smother overwintering insects and eggs.

fertilizer.recommendation: Apply a balanced fertilizer in early spring before bud break.

Peach___healthy.irrigation: Water deeply once a week during dry spells, especially during the final swell of the fruit before harvest.

pesticides: Fungicide sprays (e.g., Captan) for brown rot prevention starting a few weeks before harvest.
insecticides: Spinosad or Permethrin for oriental fruit moth and peach tree borer (trunk spray).

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: A common bacterial disease of peppers causing water-soaked spots on leaves and raised, scabby spots on fruit.
steps: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants.
Practice crop rotation; do not plant peppers, tomatoes, or eggplants in the same spot for at least 3 years.
Remove and destroy infected plants and debris promptly.
Mulch plants to prevent water from splashing from the soil onto leaves.
Sanitize tools and hands after working with infected plants.

fertilizer.recommendation: Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers. Ensure a good supply of calcium to promote healthy fruit.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.irrigation: Use drip irrigation or soaker hoses to keep foliage dry. Water in the morning.

pesticides: Copper-based bactericides (use preventatively, often mixed with mancozeb)
insecticides: Not applicable for this bacterial disease.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: The bell pepper plant appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Use black plastic mulch to warm the soil, conserve moisture, and suppress weeds.
Support plants with stakes or cages to prevent branches from breaking under the weight of the fruit.
Harvest peppers regularly by cutting the stem (don't pull) to encourage continued production.
Rotate planting locations annually to prevent soil-borne disease buildup.

fertilizer.recommendation: Use a balanced fertilizer at planting. Sidedress with a fertilizer lower in nitrogen and higher in phosphorus and potassium once fruit begins to set.
products: 5-10-10 or liquid seaweed as a sidedress

Pepper,_bell___healthy.irrigation: Provide consistent moisture (1-2 inches per week), especially during flowering and fruit set, to prevent blossom drop.

pesticides: Neem oil can be used preventatively for fungal issues.
insecticides: Insecticidal soap for aphids
Spinosad for thrips
Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) for caterpillars.

Potato___Early_blight.description: A fungal disease causing dark 'target-like' spots on potato leaves.
steps: Use certified resistant varieties when available.
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops for 3-4 years.
Maintain adequate potassium levels in the soil to reduce susceptibility.
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest.
Begin a preventative fungicide program before symptoms appear.

fertilizer.recommendation: Ensure adequate potassium (K) levels, as deficiency can increase severity. Avoid excessive nitrogen.

Potato___Early_blight.irrigation: Use drip irrigation to keep foliage dry. If using sprinklers, water in the early morning so leaves dry quickly.

insecticides: Not directly applicable, but managing pests like Colorado potato beetles reduces overall plant stress.

Potato___Late_blight.description: A destructive fungal disease that can rapidly destroy potato leaves, stems, and tubers.
steps: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes and resistant varieties like Defender or Kennebec.
Destroy cull piles and volunteer potatoes where the disease can overwinter.
Hill potatoes properly to create a soil barrier protecting tubers from spores.
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
Monitor weather conditions and apply preventative sprays before periods of cool, wet weather.

fertilizer.recommendation: Provide balanced fertility. Avoid excessive late-season nitrogen which can delay tuber maturity and increase susceptibility.

Potato___Late_blight.irrigation: Avoid overhead irrigation, especially in the evening. Water at the soil level to keep foliage dry. Ensure good soil drainage.

insecticides: Not directly applicable, but control pests like aphids that can weaken the plant.

Potato___healthy.description: The potato plant appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Hill soil around plants as they grow to protect developing tubers from sunlight (which turns them green).
Use certified disease-free seed potatoes to avoid introducing diseases.
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops (e.g., legumes, grains).
Harvest after vines have died back completely for the best storage quality.
Control weeds to reduce competition for resources.

fertilizer.recommendation: Work a balanced fertilizer into the soil at planting time.

Potato___healthy.irrigation: Provide consistent moisture, especially during tuber formation. Aim for 1-2 inches of water per week.

pesticides: Preventative copper or sulfur sprays can be used if disease pressure is high in your area.
insecticides: Neem oil for aphids and flea beetles
Spinosad or Bt for Colorado potato beetle larvae.

Raspberry___healthy.description: The raspberry plant appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Prune canes annually. For summer-bearing types, remove canes that fruited immediately after harvest. For everbearing types, prune the tops after the fall harvest.
Train canes on a trellis to improve air circulation and make harvesting easier.
Mulch with organic material to conserve moisture, suppress weeds, and add organic matter.
Remove any suckers that grow too far from the main row.

fertilizer.recommendation: Apply a balanced fertilizer in the early spring as new growth begins.

Raspberry___healthy.irrigation: Provide about 1 inch of water per week, especially during flowering and fruit development. Use drip irrigation to keep canes and leaves dry.

pesticides: Lime sulfur spray during dormancy can help prevent fungal diseases like anthracnose.
insecticides: Neem oil for aphids and spider mites
Pyrethrin for Japanese beetles.

Soybean___healthy.description: The soybean plant appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Inoculate seeds with the correct strain of Bradyrhizobium japonicum bacteria for proper nitrogen fixation, especially if soybeans have not been grown in the field before.
Test soil and maintain a pH between 6.0 and 6.8 for optimal nutrient uptake.
Use proper planting depth (1 to 1.5 inches) in moist soil for good emergence.
Practice crop rotation with non-legume crops like corn or wheat.
Scout for pests and diseases regularly throughout the growing season.

fertilizer.recommendation: Soybeans are legumes and fix their own nitrogen. Fertilizer needs are mainly for phosphorus (P) and potassium (K). Base application on a soil test.

Soybean___healthy.irrigation: Water is most critical during the flowering and pod-fill stages. Avoid drought stress during these periods to maximize yield.

pesticides: Fungicides (e.g., Pyraclostrobin) may be warranted if disease pressure is high during pod-fill stages.
insecticides: Lambda-cyhalothrin for bean leaf beetles
Bifenthrin for soybean aphids.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: A common fungal disease of squash that appears as white powdery spots on leaves and stems.
steps: Use resistant varieties whenever possible.
Provide adequate spacing between plants to ensure good air circulation.
Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves and plant debris.
Plant in a sunny location.
Apply fungicides at the first sign of disease.

fertilizer.recommendation: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer, which produces dense, susceptible foliage. Ensure good potassium levels.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.irrigation: Water the soil, not the leaves. Use drip irrigation or a soaker hose. Water in the morning.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease, but control aphids as they can spread other viruses.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: A fungal disease causing irregular purplish blotches on strawberry leaves.
steps: Use resistant varieties like Allstar, Earliglow, or Jewel.
Remove and destroy infected leaves during and after the growing season.
Practice crop rotation by establishing new beds every 3-4 years.
Improve air circulation by maintaining proper spacing and controlling weeds.
Renovate beds after harvest by mowing off old leaves.

fertilizer.recommendation: Apply fertilizer after renovation in the summer, not in the spring, to avoid promoting soft growth susceptible to disease.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.irrigation: Water early in the day so foliage has time to dry completely. Use drip irrigation.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Strawberry___healthy.description: The strawberry plant appears to be healthy. The following are general care recommendations.
steps: Renovate beds annually after harvest by mowing the leaves, narrowing the rows, and topdressing with compost.
Use mulch (like straw) to conserve moisture, suppress weeds, and keep ripening fruits clean.
Replace plants every 3-4 years for maximum productivity and to reduce disease buildup.
Protect blossoms from late spring frosts with row covers.

fertilizer.recommendation: Fertilize after renovation in summer and again in late fall. Avoid heavy spring fertilization.

Strawberry___healthy.irrigation: Provide 1-2 inches of water per week, especially during runner production and fruit development. The root system is shallow.

pesticides: Sulfur can be used to prevent powdery mildew.
insecticides: Insecticidal soap for aphids and spider mites
Spinosad for fruit worms.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease causing small, water-soaked spots on tomato leaves and fruit.
steps: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants.
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops for 2-3 years.
Space plants properly to ensure good air circulation and fast drying.
Apply mulch to prevent bacteria from splashing from the soil onto the plants.
Sanitize stakes, cages, and tools.

fertilizer.recommendation: Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen. Ensure adequate calcium levels.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.irrigation: Use drip irrigation or soaker hoses to keep foliage dry. Water in the morning.

pesticides: Copper-based bactericides (often mixed with mancozeb for better efficacy)
insecticides: Not applicable for this bacterial disease.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A fungal disease of tomatoes, common in greenhouses, that causes pale green or yellow spots on the upper leaf surface and olive-green mold on the underside.
steps: Reduce humidity by ensuring proper spacing and good ventilation, especially in greenhouses.
Use resistant varieties like Bush Beefsteak or Valley Girl.
Water at the base of plants to avoid wetting foliage.
Remove and destroy infected leaves promptly.
Prune lower leaves to increase airflow.

fertilizer.recommendation: Maintain balanced nutrition to keep plants vigorous.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.irrigation: Water early in the day using drip irrigation to minimize leaf wetness and humidity.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A common fungal disease of tomatoes causing numerous small spots with dark borders and tan centers on the leaves.
steps: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves as they appear.
Apply mulch to create a barrier between the soil and the plant leaves.
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops for at least 3 years.
Stake or cage plants to improve air circulation.
Sanitize tools and cages at the end of the season.

fertilizer.recommendation: Ensure the plant is well-fed but avoid excessive nitrogen.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.irrigation: Use drip irrigation or a soaker hose. Avoid overhead watering to keep leaves dry.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: A common pest of tomatoes, spider mites cause stippling on leaves and can create fine webbing on the plant.
steps: Spray plants with a strong jet of water, especially on the underside of leaves, to dislodge mites.
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) as a biological control.
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural mite predators.
Remove heavily infested leaves or plants.
Increase humidity, as mites thrive in hot, dry conditions.

fertilizer.recommendation: Healthy plants are more tolerant. Avoid drought stress, which favors mite outbreaks.
products: Liquid seaweed extract to help with stress.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.irrigation: Maintain consistent soil moisture. Periodically hosing down the plant can help control mite populations.

pesticides: This is a pest, not a disease. Use miticides if necessary.
insecticides: Abamectin
Bifenazate
Horticultural oil
Insecticidal soap (effective on contact)

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease causing small, water-soaked spots that develop into larger lesions with distinct concentric rings, resembling a target.
steps: Remove and destroy infected leaves and fruits.
Stake or cage plants to improve air circulation and keep fruit off the ground.
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops.
Apply mulch to prevent soil splashing onto plants.
Follow a preventative fungicide spray program.

fertilizer.recommendation: Maintain balanced nutrition. Ensure adequate potassium.

Tomato___Target_Spot.irrigation: Water at the soil level using drip irrigation. Keep foliage as dry as possible.

insecticides: Not applicable for this fungal disease.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A viral disease transmitted by whiteflies, causing severe stunting, upward curling of leaves, and yellowing of leaf margins.
steps: Use resistant varieties like Tycoon, Security, or Talladega.
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly to reduce the source of the virus.
Use reflective (silver) mulches to repel whiteflies.
Use floating row covers to exclude whiteflies from young plants.
Manage weeds in and around the garden, as they can host whiteflies.

fertilizer.recommendation: Provide balanced nutrition to support the plant, but there is no fertilizer cure for the virus.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.irrigation: Maintain consistent moisture to support stressed plants.

pesticides: There is no cure for the virus. Control is focused on the insect vector.
insecticides: Imidacloprid (systemic, applied to soil)
Neem oil
Insecticidal soap
Pyrethrin
Spinosad

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A viral disease causing mottled light and dark green patterns on tomato leaves, often leading to stunted growth.
steps: Use certified virus-free seeds and transplants.
Disinfect tools, stakes, and hands regularly with a bleach solution or milk.
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
Avoid smoking (cigarettes/tobacco) around tomato plants as tobacco can carry the virus.
Control aphids, which can transmit the virus.

fertilizer.recommendation: There is no fertilizer cure. Focus on balanced nutrition for overall plant health.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.irrigation: Provide regular watering to prevent stress.

pesticides: There is no cure for the virus. Control is focused on prevention and vector management.
insecticides: Insecticidal soap or Neem oil to control aphid populations.
